title: The Threat of the Flower
text:
Flower of the poppies:

deceive me and do not love me.


How you exaggerate your aroma,

how far you carry your blush,

flower that paints dark circles on yourself

and exhales your soul to the sun!


Flower of the poppies.


One woman resembled you

in the blush with which you deceive,

and also because she had,

like you, black lashes.


Flower of the poppies.

One woman resembled you...

And I tremble only to see

your hand placed in mine:

I tremble lest a day should dawn

when you become a woman!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the playful refrain and the uneasy transformation from flower to woman.

title: Absences
text:
Of the friends I loved most

and who in a brief span have abandoned me,

the shadows slip beside me,

scant relief to my melancholy.


Their voices mingle with mine

and I see myself suspended and sleepless

in the effort to cross the ford

that separates me from their company.


I yield to the intoxicating invitation,

and reason that time turns back

and refines an infinity each hour.


And I overflow the limits, so that

my feeling explores immensity

and I become familiar with death.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the sonnet's movement from lost friends toward intimacy with death.

title: Visitation
text:
—I am Death— she told me. I did not know

that she hemmed me in so closely,

to the point of pouring over my face

her troubling cold breath.


I no longer try to elude her company:

she follows my steps, transparent and clear,

and since then she does not forsake me

or leave me by night or by day.


—And to think —I confessed— that in a thousand ways

I tried to disguise you with nicknames,

confused amid fears and errors!


"You have more of caress than of grief."

You were relief and I called you chain.

You were death and I called you life.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the direct encounter with Death and the final reversal of names.

title: Stay Silent
text:
Stay silent and alone:

almost everything is excess and needless.

From the branch hangs the fruit

and from the pedicel the rose,

not only for the purposes of desire,

but for the inert blindness

that vision exaggerates

in reach and in meaning;

and what you sing asleep

is your true song.


Stay alone and silent:

almost everything is needless and excess.

No expense is recovered,

nor is the exchanged gold worth

the coin you have paid

for heaps of fleece.

For by thefts the heart gives

the beats you make use of,

and though you imagine you pay,

you owe it to the pantheon.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the moral aphorism and the reversal of needless excess.

title: Havana
text:
It is not Cuba, where the sea dissolves the soul.

It is not Cuba —which Gauguin never saw,

Which Picasso never saw—,

Where Black people dressed in yellow and cherry red

Roam the seawall, between two lights,

And defeated eyes

No longer disguise their thoughts.


It is not Cuba — the one that heard Stravinsky

Arrange sounds of marimbas and güiros

At the burial of Papá Montero,

Ñañigo with cane and rumbero scoundrel.


It is not Cuba — where the colonial Yankee

Cures himself of the sultriness sipping "granizados"

Of breeze, on the terraces of the development;

Where the police disinfect

The sting of the last mosquitoes

That still buzz in Spanish.


It is not Cuba — where the sea becomes transparent

So the wreckage of the Maine will not be lost,

And a revolutionary contractor

Tints the afternoon air white,

Fanning, with veteran smile,

From his rocking chair, the fragrance

Of custom-house coconuts and mangoes.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the satirical catalogue of Cuba, Havana, empire, music, and memory.

title: As Evening Declines, the Friends Draw Near
text:
As evening declines, the friends draw near;

but the little voice does not stop crying.

We close the windows, the doors, the shutters,

but the drop of sorrow keeps falling.


We do not know where the little voice comes from;

we search the farm, the stable, the hayloft.

The field dozes in the warmth of the soft sun,

but the little voice does not stop crying.


—The creaking waterwheel!— say the sharpest ones.

But there are no waterwheels here! What a singular thing!

They stare at one another, astonished, and grow mute

because the little voice does not stop crying.


What had been laughter is now open unease

and a vague malaise takes hold of everyone,

and all take leave and escape in haste,

because the little voice does not stop crying.


When night arrives, the sky is already a sob

and even the wood of the hearth feigns a sob.

Alone, without speaking, we weep behind a cloak,

but the little voice does not stop crying.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the ballad-like refrain of the unstoppable little voice.

title: The Miller's Daughter
text:
That is the girl of the mill

and so lovely, so lovely she became,

that

I would like to be the earring

that trembles in her ear:

for,

hidden in her curls night and day,

I would brush her warm white neck.


I would like to be the belt

of her waist so fine, so fine:

her

heart would beat its pulses against me,

sorrowful or glad;

if it beats

as it should I would know,

embracing her waist, always very tight.

I would like

to be a necklace

and so sway all day

on her fragrant breast,


one with her laughter and her sighs:

and so light, so light there

I would be,

that at night she would barely unfasten me.


Version by Màrie Manent
editorial_note: The translation follows the Spanish version's intimate sequence of earring, belt, and necklace.

title: It Is Well and It Is Something: We Can Stop...
text:
The Miller's Daughter


That is the girl of the mill

and so lovely, so lovely she became,

that

I would like to be the earring

that trembles in her ear:

for,

hidden in her curls night and day,

I would brush her warm white neck.


I would like to be the belt

of her waist so fine, so fine:

her

heart would beat its pulses against me,

sorrowful or glad;

if it beats

as it should I would know,

embracing her waist, always very tight.

I would like

to be a necklace

and so sway all day

on her fragrant breast,


one with her laughter and her sighs:

and so light, so light there

I would be,

that at night she would barely unfasten me.


Version by Màrie Manent
editorial_note: The catalog title differs from the embedded poem, so the internal Miller's Daughter heading is preserved.

title: After the Rain
text:
Through the flowered ravines

Last night the downpour passed

And the lemon tree dawned

Weeping little white stars.


Lost cowbells wander

Among fresh grasslands,

And the wintery mists pass,

Erasing hills.
editorial_note: The translation keeps Espino's rural clarity and the lemon tree's starry tears.

title: Plumbago
text:
Chiaroscuro, the river sings!

How does it come so playfully?

And the leaves with dew

are green eyes crying!


What celestial music

is heard in these places;

murmurings of banana groves

and of wild doves!


Among the mountain fineries

everything is a lyre:

the turtle-dove that sighs

is a madrigal with wings!
editorial_note: The translation keeps the bright musical pastoral of river, grove, and dove.
